title: Computational Complexity and Speedup Factors Analyses for Self-Suspending Tasks

extraction.paper_name: Computational Complexity and Speedup Factors Analyses for Self-Suspending Tasks
extraction.paper_description: This paper analyzes the computational complexity and speedup factors of schedulability analysis for self-suspending sporadic tasks under fixed-priority (FP) and other scheduling algorithms. It proves that schedulability analysis for FP with segmented self-suspending tasks is coN P-hard in the strong sense. It also demonstrates that speedup factors for FP, EDF, LLF, and EDZL are unbounded for dynamic self-suspending tasks if suspension times cannot be reduced, but shows constant speedup factors under suspension-coherent speeding up or small suspension times.

formal_description.statement:
A sporadic real-time task tau_i is characterized by the tuple (C_i, S_i, D_i, T_i). Each job of task tau_i, denoted by tau_i_j, is released at time r_i_j and has an absolute deadline at time d_i_j. 
- C_i: worst-case execution time.
- S_i: worst-case self-suspension time (across all suspension phases).
- D_i: relative deadline.
- T_i: period (or minimum inter-arrival time).

For each job tau_i_j: d_i_j = r_i_j + D_i and r_i_j_plus_1 >= r_i_j + T_i.

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.S_i: worst-case self-suspension time of task i
variables.T_i: minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task i
variables.r_i_j: release time of j-th job of task i
variables.d_i_j: absolute deadline of j-th job of task i
variables.r_i_j_plus_1: release time of (j+1)-th job of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental parameters and timing constraints for a sporadic self-suspending task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Each task has a maximum computation time (C_i), a maximum time it can pause itself (S_i), a deadline relative to its release (D_i), and a minimum time between its releases (T_i). Jobs must finish by their absolute deadline (release time + relative deadline).
steps: Identify task properties: C_i, S_i, D_i, T_i.
Understand job release and deadline: d_i_j = r_i_j + D_i.
Understand minimum inter-arrival: r_i_j_plus_1 >= r_i_j + T_i.
Note the constraints: C_i, S_i are positive, S_i is less than D_i, and total work (C_i + S_i) must fit within D_i.
key_insights: These parameters define the workload and timing requirements of a task.
Self-suspension (S_i) is a distinct component from execution (C_i) and impacts schedulability.

formal_description.statement: A task set T is called an implicit-deadline task set if the relative deadline D_i of task tau_i is always equal to its period T_i for every task tau_i in T.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific type of task set where deadlines are equal to periods.

informal_sketch.intuition: In an implicit-deadline system, tasks must complete within their period. This simplifies analysis compared to constrained or arbitrary deadlines.
steps: For every task tau_i in the set T, check if D_i == T_i.
If this holds for all tasks, the set is implicit-deadline.
key_insights: Simplifies schedulability analysis as deadlines align with release patterns.
Often used as a baseline for theoretical results.

formal_description.statement: A task set T is called a constrained-deadline task set if the relative deadline D_i of task tau_i is always no more than its period T_i (D_i <= T_i) for every task tau_i in T.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific type of task set where deadlines are less than or equal to periods.

informal_sketch.intuition: In a constrained-deadline system, tasks must complete within their period or earlier. This is a common and practical scenario, more general than implicit-deadline.
steps: For every task tau_i in the set T, check if D_i <= T_i.
If this holds for all tasks, the set is constrained-deadline.
key_insights: More general than implicit-deadline, allowing deadlines to be shorter than periods.
Still simpler to analyze than arbitrary deadlines (D_i > T_i).

formal_description.statement: The dynamic self-suspension model allows a job of task tau_i to suspend itself at any moment before it finishes as long as the worst-case self-suspension time S_i is not violated.

variables.S_i: worst-case self-suspension time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a flexible self-suspension model where suspension can occur dynamically.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task can decide to suspend itself at any point during its execution, as long as the total suspension time for that job doesn't exceed its maximum allowed (S_i). The exact timing of suspensions is not predefined.
steps: A job starts execution.
It can pause (suspend) at any time, releasing the processor.
It can resume later.
The total duration of all such pauses for one job must not exceed S_i.
key_insights: Offers high flexibility for system designers.
Can lead to pessimistic schedulability analysis due to the unknown suspension pattern.

formal_description.statement: The segmented self-suspension model characterizes the computation segments and suspension intervals as an array (C_1_i, S_1_i, C_2_i, S_2_i, ..., S_m_i_minus_1_i, C_m_i_i), composed of m_i computation segments separated by m_i - 1 suspension intervals.

variables.C_j_i: j-th computation segment of task i
variables.S_j_i: j-th suspension interval of task i
variables.m_i: number of computation segments for task i

assumptions: The total execution time sum_{j=1}^{m_i} C_j_i equals C_i.
The total suspension time sum_{j=1}^{m_i-1} S_j_i equals S_i.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a structured self-suspension model with predefined execution and suspension patterns.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task's execution is broken into a fixed sequence of computation blocks and suspension periods. For example, compute, then suspend, then compute again. The lengths of these blocks and suspensions are known.
steps: Define a sequence of (computation, suspension) pairs.
A job executes C_1_i, then suspends for S_1_i, then executes C_2_i, and so on.
The last segment is always a computation segment C_m_i_i.
key_insights: Provides more precise information about suspension behavior.
Can lead to less pessimistic analysis than dynamic self-suspension if patterns are well-defined.

formal_description.statement: The utilization of a task tau_i is defined as U_i = C_i / T_i.

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the processor utilization for a single task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Utilization represents the fraction of processor time that a task ideally requires. If a task needs C_i time units every T_i period, its utilization is C_i/T_i.
steps: Divide the worst-case execution time (C_i) by the task's period (T_i).
The result is a dimensionless value, typically between 0 and 1.
key_insights: A fundamental metric in real-time systems to quantify processor load.
Total utilization (sum of U_i for all tasks) is a necessary condition for schedulability (must be <= 1 for a single processor).

formal_description.statement: A schedule is feasible if all the temporal characteristics and timing constraints are respected and satisfied.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines what constitutes a valid schedule.

informal_sketch.intuition: A schedule is 'feasible' if every task completes its execution before its deadline, and all other system rules (like minimum inter-arrival times, suspension limits) are followed.
steps: For every job of every task:
Check if its execution completes by its absolute deadline.
Check if its suspension time does not exceed S_i.
Check if its release time respects T_i.
If all checks pass, the schedule is feasible.
key_insights: The ultimate goal of real-time scheduling is to produce feasible schedules.
Feasibility implies meeting all timing requirements, not just deadlines.

formal_description.statement: A task system (set) is schedulable by a scheduling algorithm if the resulting schedule is always feasible.

variables.scheduling_algorithm: the algorithm used to schedule tasks

formal_description.conclusion: Defines when a task system can be successfully managed by an algorithm.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task system is 'schedulable' by a given algorithm if that algorithm can *always* find a feasible schedule for *any* valid sequence of job releases from that task system.
steps: Consider all possible valid job release patterns for the task system.
For each pattern, apply the scheduling_algorithm to generate a schedule.
Check if every generated schedule is feasible (using the 'Feasible Schedule' definition).
If all are feasible, the task system is schedulable by the algorithm.
key_insights: Schedulability is a property of the task system *and* the scheduling algorithm.
It implies robustness against all valid worst-case scenarios.

formal_description.statement:
A schedulability test of a scheduling algorithm for a given task system is to validate whether the task system is schedulable by the scheduling algorithm.
- Sufficient schedulability test: Provides only sufficient conditions for validating schedulability.
- Necessary schedulability test: Provides only necessary conditions to allow schedulability.
- Exact schedulability test: Provides necessary and sufficient conditions for validating schedulability.

variables.scheduling_algorithm: the algorithm used to schedule tasks

formal_description.conclusion: Defines methods for verifying if a task system is schedulable and categorizes their completeness.

informal_sketch.intuition: A schedulability test is a procedure to determine if a task system will always meet its deadlines under a specific scheduling algorithm. Tests can be 'sufficient' (if it passes, it's schedulable, but if it fails, it might still be schedulable), 'necessary' (if it fails, it's definitely not schedulable, but if it passes, it might still not be schedulable), or 'exact' (passes if and only if schedulable).
steps: Input: a task system and a scheduling algorithm.
Output: a boolean (schedulable/not schedulable) or a condition.
Sufficient: If test_passes -> schedulable. If test_fails -> unknown.
Necessary: If test_passes -> unknown. If test_fails -> not_schedulable.
Exact: If test_passes <-> schedulable.
key_insights: Exact tests are ideal but often computationally expensive.
Sufficient and necessary tests are used when exact tests are not available or too complex.

formal_description.statement:
If an algorithm A has a speedup factor rho, then it guarantees that the schedule derived from the algorithm A is always feasible by running at speed rho, if the input task set admits a feasible schedule on a unit-speed processor.

Negation: If algorithm A fails to provide a feasible schedule for an input task system, then there does not exist any feasible schedule (in the worst cases) for the task set when the execution time of each task tau_i in T (running at speed 1/rho) becomes rho * C_i. The self-suspension time S_i is NOT reduced by speeding up.

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i

assumptions: Suspension length cannot be reduced by speeding up.
formal_description.conclusion: Quantifies the theoretical quality of a scheduling algorithm by how much faster a processor needs to be to guarantee schedulability, assuming suspension times are fixed.

informal_sketch.intuition: A speedup factor of 'rho' means that if a task set can be scheduled by an optimal algorithm on a standard processor, then our algorithm 'A' can schedule it if the processor runs 'rho' times faster. This is a way to measure how 'bad' an algorithm is: a higher rho means it needs a faster processor.
steps: Assume an optimal scheduler can schedule a task set T on a unit-speed processor.
If algorithm A can schedule T on a processor of speed 'rho' (meaning all C_i become C_i / rho), then A has a speedup factor of 'rho'.
Alternatively, if A fails to schedule T on a unit-speed processor, then no optimal scheduler could schedule T if all C_i were scaled up by 'rho' (i.e., processor speed 1/rho).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_speedup_factor(algorithm_A, task_set):
    # This is a theoretical bound, not a direct calculation
    # It involves finding the minimum 'rho' such that:
    # if optimal_schedule_exists(task_set, speed=1):
    #     return algorithm_A.can_schedule(task_set, speed=rho)
    pass
key_insights: A lower speedup factor indicates a better algorithm.
A speedup factor of 1 means the algorithm is optimal.
This definition assumes suspension times are invariant to processor speed.

formal_description.statement: If algorithm A fails to provide a feasible schedule for an input task system, then there does not exist any feasible schedule (in the worst cases) for the task set when the execution time of each task tau_i in T (running at speed 1/rho) becomes rho * C_i AND the self-suspension time of each task tau_i in T (suspending at speed 1/rho) becomes rho * S_i.

variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i
variables.S_i: worst-case self-suspension time of task i

assumptions: Suspension length can also be coherently reduced by speeding up.
formal_description.conclusion: Quantifies the theoretical quality of a scheduling algorithm by how much faster a processor needs to be to guarantee schedulability, assuming both execution and suspension times scale with processor speed.

informal_sketch.intuition: Similar to the standard speedup factor, but here, if the processor speeds up by 'rho', both the computation time (C_i) and the suspension time (S_i) of tasks are effectively reduced by a factor of 'rho'. This models scenarios where the cause of suspension (e.g., synchronization) also benefits from faster hardware.
steps: Assume algorithm A fails to schedule a task set T on a unit-speed processor.
Then, no optimal scheduler could schedule T if all C_i were scaled up by 'rho' AND all S_i were scaled up by 'rho' (i.e., processor speed 1/rho).
key_insights: This model is more optimistic for schedulability as both execution and suspension benefit from faster hardware.
Relevant for systems where suspension is due to internal processor-related delays.

formal_description.statement:
Given a positive integer V, a positive integer M, and a set of 3M integer numbers {v_2, v_3, ..., v_3M_plus_1} with the condition sum_{i=2}^{3M_plus_1} v_i = M * V, in which V/4 < v_i < V/2 and M >= 3. 
Objective: The problem is to partition the given 3M integer numbers into M disjoint sets V_1, V_2, ..., V_M such that the sum of the numbers in each set V_i for i = 1, 2, ..., M is V, i.e., sum_{v_j in V_i} v_j = V.

variables.V_i: a disjoint set in the partition

assumptions: M is a positive integer, M >= 3.
V/4 < v_i < V/2 for all v_i.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the 3-PARTITION problem, which is NP-complete in the strong sense and used for reduction proofs.

informal_sketch.intuition: Imagine you have 3M items, each with a specific weight (v_i). You want to divide these items into M bins, such that each bin has exactly 3 items, and the total weight in each bin is exactly V. The problem is to determine if such a division is possible.
steps: Given a list of 3M numbers and a target sum V.
Try to group the numbers into M sets.
Each set must contain exactly 3 numbers (implied by the sum and range constraints).
The sum of numbers in each set must be V.
All sets must be disjoint and cover all 3M numbers.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def solve_3_partition(V, M, v_numbers):
    # This is an NP-hard problem, no efficient general solution
    # Typically solved with backtracking or approximation algorithms
    # For this context, we just need to know its complexity.
    pass
key_insights: This problem is known to be computationally very hard (NP-complete in the strong sense).
It's often used in complexity proofs by showing that if you could solve a specific schedulability problem efficiently, you could also solve 3-PARTITION efficiently, which is unlikely.

results.identifier: Definition 2 (Reduction to a constrained-deadline system T_red)

formal_description.statement:
For a given input instance of the 3-PARTITION problem (V, M, {v_i}), we construct n = 3MV + 2 sporadic tasks as follows, forming task set T_red:
- Task tau_1: C_1 = V, S_1 = 0, D_1 = V, T_1 = 3V.
- For task tau_i with i = 2, ..., 3M + 1: C_i = v_i, S_i = 0, T_i = 21MV.
  - D_i = 3MV/2 if M is an even number.
  - D_i = 3MV/2 + V/2 if M is an odd number.
- For task tau_3M_plus_2: A segmented self-suspending task with m_3M_plus_2 = M computation segments separated by M - 1 self-suspension intervals.
  - C_j_3M_plus_2 = V + 1 for j = 1, ..., M.
  - S_j_3M_plus_2 = 6V for j = 1, ..., M - 1.
  - D_3M_plus_2 = M * (4V + 1) - V + 6V * (M - 1) = 10MV + M - 7V.
  - T_3M_plus_2 = 21MV.

Priority Assignment: tau_1 is highest priority. Tasks tau_2, ..., tau_3M_plus_1 have lower priorities than tau_1 and higher priorities than tau_3M_plus_2. (Order among tau_2 to tau_3M_plus_1 is arbitrary).
formal_description.conclusion: Constructs a specific constrained-deadline task system with a segmented self-suspending task, designed to be schedulable if and only if the 3-PARTITION instance has a solution.

informal_sketch.intuition: This definition creates a special set of tasks (T_red) from a 3-PARTITION problem. The idea is that the schedulability of the lowest-priority task (tau_3M_plus_2) will depend directly on whether the 3-PARTITION problem has a solution. If the 3-PARTITION can be solved, tau_3M_plus_2 will miss its deadline, and vice-versa.
steps: Take the parameters (V, M, v_i) from a 3-PARTITION instance.
Create a high-priority task (tau_1) with specific C, D, T.
Create 3M intermediate-priority tasks (tau_2 to tau_3M_plus_1), each corresponding to a v_i, with specific C, D, T.
Create a low-priority segmented self-suspending task (tau_3M_plus_2) with M segments, each with specific C_j, S_j, D, T.
Assign priorities: tau_1 > {tau_2...tau_3M_plus_1} > tau_3M_plus_2.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def construct_task_set_T_red(V, M, v_numbers):
    task_set = []

    # Task tau_1
    task_1 = Task(C=V, S=0, D=V, T=3*V)
    task_set.append(task_1)

    # Tasks tau_2 to tau_3M_plus_1
    for i in range(len(v_numbers)):
        v_i = v_numbers[i]
        D_i = (3*M*V/2) if (M % 2 == 0) else (3*M*V/2 + V/2)
        task_i_plus_1 = Task(C=v_i, S=0, D=D_i, T=21*M*V)
        task_set.append(task_i_plus_1)

    # Task tau_3M_plus_2
    segments_3M_plus_2 = []
    for j in range(M):
        C_j = V + 1
        S_j = 6*V if j < M - 1 else 0 # Last segment has no suspension after it
        segments_3M_plus_2.append((C_j, S_j))
    D_3M_plus_2 = M * (4*V + 1) - V + 6*V * (M - 1)
    T_3M_plus_2 = 21*M*V
    task_3M_plus_2 = SegmentedSelfSuspendingTask(segments_3M_plus_2, D_3M_plus_2, T_3M_plus_2)
    task_set.append(task_3M_plus_2)

    return task_set
key_insights: This reduction is the core of the coN P-hardness proof.
The specific parameters are chosen to create a tight relationship between 3-PARTITION solutions and schedulability.

formal_description.statement:
For the j-th computation segment C_j_3M_plus_2 of task tau_3M_plus_2, let T_j be the set of tasks from {tau_2, ..., tau_3M_plus_1} released together with C_j_3M_plus_2, and let w_j = sum_{tau_i in T_j} C_i. The response time R_w_j of this computation segment (after its release) is defined as the minimum t > 0 such that:
C_j_3M_plus_2 + w_j + ceil(t / T_1) * C_1 <= t

Given C_j_3M_plus_2 = V + 1, C_1 = V, T_1 = 3V, this becomes:
V + 1 + w_j + ceil(t / (3V)) * V <= t

The solution for R_w_j is piecewise:
R_w_j = 
  2V + 1 + w_j                 if w_j <= V - 1
  4V + 1                       if w_j = V
  V + 1 + w_j + floor((V + 1 + w_j) / (2V)) * V if w_j > V

variables.R_w_j: response time of the j-th computation segment of tau_3M_plus_2, given w_j
variables.w_j: sum of execution times of higher-priority tasks (from tau_2 to tau_3M_plus_1) released with C_j_3M_plus_2
variables.C_j_3M_plus_2: execution time of j-th segment of tau_3M_plus_2

assumptions: Worst-case release pattern as described in Lemma 4.
tau_1 is the only higher-priority task that can interfere periodically.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the worst-case response time for a single computation segment of the lowest-priority task tau_3M_plus_2, considering interference from higher-priority tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: This formula calculates how long it takes for a specific computation segment of the lowest-priority task (tau_3M_plus_2) to finish, given a certain amount of interference (w_j) from intermediate-priority tasks and periodic interference from the highest-priority task (tau_1). The piecewise nature arises from how the periodic interference from tau_1 accumulates over time.
steps: The response time (R_w_j) is the sum of the segment's own execution (V+1), the one-time interference (w_j), and the periodic interference from tau_1.
The periodic interference from tau_1 is `ceil(R_w_j / T_1) * C_1`.
This forms a recursive equation `R_w_j = (V + 1) + w_j + ceil(R_w_j / (3V)) * V`.
The piecewise definition provides the closed-form solution for this equation based on the value of w_j.
key_insights: This function is crucial for determining if tau_3M_plus_2 meets its deadline.
The specific values (V, 3V, 2V) are carefully chosen to create a sensitive relationship with the 3-PARTITION problem.

dependencies: Definition 2 (Reduction to a constrained-deadline system T_red)

formal_description.statement:
If a constrained-deadline dynamic self-suspension sporadic task system T is schedulable under a scheduling algorithm, then for all t > 0:
sum_{tau_i in T} max(0, floor((t - (D_i - S_i)) / T_i) + 1) * C_i <= t

variables.S_i: worst-case self-suspension time of task i
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i

assumptions: System is schedulable under *any* scheduling algorithm.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a necessary condition for schedulability, meaning if this inequality is violated for any 't', the task system is definitely not schedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma states that the total demand for processor time by all tasks, considering their deadlines and suspension times, must not exceed the available time 't'. It's a generalization of the utilization bound, accounting for deadlines and suspensions.
steps: For a given time interval 't', calculate the maximum possible execution demand from each task tau_i.
The term `D_i - S_i` represents the effective deadline for the *execution* part of task tau_i, assuming suspension happens as late as possible.
The `floor((t - (D_i - S_i)) / T_i) + 1` part counts the maximum number of jobs of task tau_i that could demand execution within 't' and have their effective deadline within 't'.
Sum these demands for all tasks.
If this total demand exceeds 't' for any 't', then the system cannot be scheduled.
key_insights: This is a fundamental lower bound on processor capacity required for schedulability.
It's a necessary condition, so passing it doesn't guarantee schedulability, but failing it guarantees non-schedulability.
The `D_i - S_i` term is critical for self-suspending tasks, as it effectively shortens the available time for computation.

formal_description.statement:
If a constrained-deadline dynamic self-suspension sporadic task system T is schedulable under a fixed-priority preemptive scheduling algorithm, then, for each task tau_k:
exists 0 < t <= D_k, s.t. C_k + S_k + sum_{tau_i in hp(tau_k)} ceil(t / T_i) * C_i <= t

variables.C_k: worst-case execution time of task k
variables.S_k: worst-case self-suspension time of task k
variables.hp_tau_k: set of tasks with higher priority than task k
variables.C_i: worst-case execution time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a necessary condition for schedulability under fixed-priority scheduling, focusing on the response time of individual tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma states that for any task tau_k to be schedulable under fixed-priority, there must be some time 't' (within its deadline) where its own execution (C_k), its suspension (S_k), and all interference from higher-priority tasks (hp(tau_k)) can be accommodated. This is a variant of the classic response time analysis equation, adapted for self-suspension.
steps: For a specific task tau_k, iterate through possible time intervals 't' from 0 up to D_k.
For each 't', calculate the total demand: tau_k's own execution (C_k), its suspension (S_k), and the cumulative interference from all higher-priority tasks.
The interference from a higher-priority task tau_i is `ceil(t / T_i) * C_i`, representing the maximum execution it can demand in 't'.
If for any 't' in the range, the total demand is less than or equal to 't', then this necessary condition is met for tau_k.
If no such 't' exists, tau_k (and thus the system) is not schedulable.
key_insights: This condition is a direct extension of standard fixed-priority response time analysis to include self-suspension.
The `S_k` term is added to the left side, effectively increasing the 'work' that needs to be completed by time 't', reflecting that suspension time also consumes part of the task's deadline budget.
It's a necessary condition, not sufficient, as it doesn't account for all complex interactions of self-suspension.

results.identifier: Lemma 3 (Schedulability of higher-priority tasks in T_red)

formal_description.statement: Tasks tau_1, tau_2, ..., tau_3M_plus_1 in T_red can meet their deadlines under the specified FP scheduling.

variables.T_red: the constructed task set from Definition 2

assumptions: Fixed-priority scheduling as specified in Definition 2.
Task tau_3M_plus_2 (lowest priority) has no impact on higher-priority tasks.
formal_description.conclusion: The higher and intermediate priority tasks in the constructed task set T_red are always schedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: The tasks tau_1 through tau_3M_plus_1 are designed to be simple non-suspending tasks. Their parameters (C_i, D_i, T_i) are chosen such that even with interference from higher-priority tasks, they will always meet their deadlines. The lowest-priority self-suspending task (tau_3M_plus_2) cannot affect them.
steps: For tau_1: C_1 = V, D_1 = V. Since C_1 <= D_1 and it's the highest priority, it's trivially schedulable.

For tau_i (i = 2 to 3M+1): These tasks are non-suspending. Their schedulability is checked using standard fixed-priority response time analysis, considering interference from tau_1 and other higher-priority tau_j tasks.
The paper states `C_i + sum_{j=1}^{i-1} ceil(D_i / T_j) * C_j <= D_i` is satisfied due to the specific parameter choices in Definition 2.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_lemma_3(T_red):
    # Task tau_1 is highest priority, C_1 = D_1 = V, S_1 = 0
    # It's trivially schedulable.
    # For tasks tau_2 to tau_3M_plus_1:
    # These are non-suspending tasks. Their schedulability can be verified
    # using standard fixed-priority response time analysis (e.g., Liu & Layland).
    # The paper asserts this holds due to the parameter choices.
    return True # All higher-priority tasks are schedulable
key_insights: This lemma simplifies the complexity proof by ensuring that only the lowest-priority task's schedulability is in question.
The parameters of tau_1 to tau_3M_plus_1 are 'well-behaved' to isolate the complexity to tau_3M_plus_2.

dependencies: Definition 2 (Reduction to a constrained-deadline system T_red)

results.identifier: Lemma 4 (Worst-case response time conditions for tau_3M_plus_2)

formal_description.statement:
The worst-case response time of task tau_3M_plus_2 in T_red under FP scheduling happens under the following necessary conditions:
1) Task tau_3M_plus_2 releases a job at time 0. This job requests the worst-case execution time per computation segment and suspends in each self-suspension interval exactly equal to its worst case.
2) Task tau_1 always releases one job together with each computation segment of the job (released at time 0) of task tau_3M_plus_2, and releases the subsequent jobs strictly periodically with period 3V until a computation segment of task tau_3M_plus_2 finishes. Task tau_1 never releases any job when task tau_3M_plus_2 suspends itself.
3) For i = 2, 3, ..., 3M + 1, task tau_i only releases one job together with one of the M computation segments of the job (released at time 0) of task tau_3M_plus_2.

All the jobs and all the computation segments are executed with their worst-case execution time specifications.

variables.T_red: the constructed task set from Definition 2

informal_sketch.intuition: To find out if the lowest-priority task (tau_3M_plus_2) can ever miss its deadline, we need to consider the 'worst-case scenario' for its interference. This lemma describes that worst-case: all tasks arrive at the most inconvenient times, maximizing the blocking and preemption experienced by tau_3M_plus_2.
steps: tau_3M_plus_2's job starts at time 0 and uses all its worst-case execution and suspension times.

tau_1 (highest priority) releases a job exactly when each of tau_3M_plus_2's computation segments starts, and then continues to release periodically, but *only* when tau_3M_plus_2 is computing (not suspending).
Each intermediate-priority task (tau_2 to tau_3M_plus_1) releases exactly one job, and this job arrives precisely with one of tau_3M_plus_2's computation segments.
All tasks execute for their worst-case times.

The specific release pattern is designed to maximize interference on tau_3M_plus_2's computation segments.

results.identifier: Lemma 6 (Sum of R_w_j for specific w_j)

formal_description.statement: If w_1 = w_2 = ... = w_M = V, then sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j = M * (4V + 1).

variables.w_j: sum of execution times of higher-priority tasks released with C_j_3M_plus_2
variables.R_w_j: response time of the j-th computation segment of tau_3M_plus_2

formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the total response time for tau_3M_plus_2's computation segments under a specific, balanced distribution of intermediate-priority interference.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma calculates the total time tau_3M_plus_2 would spend executing its computation segments if the interference from the intermediate-priority tasks (tau_2 to tau_3M_plus_1) was perfectly balanced across all M segments, with each segment receiving exactly 'V' units of interference. It uses the R_w_j formula for the case where w_j = V.
steps: For each segment j, w_j is set to V.
Using the R_w_j formula, when w_j = V, R_w_j = 4V + 1.
Since there are M such segments, the total sum is M * (4V + 1).
key_insights: This provides a baseline for the total response time when the intermediate-priority tasks are 'perfectly' partitioned.
It's a key value for comparison in the complexity proof.

results.identifier: Lemma 7 (Upper bound on sum of R_w_j when some w_j = V)

formal_description.statement: For any non-negative integer assignment for w_1, w_2, ..., w_M with sum_{i=1}^{M} w_i = M * V, if there exists a certain index j with w_j = V, then sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j <= M * (4V + 1) - V.

variables.w_j: sum of execution times of higher-priority tasks released with C_j_3M_plus_2
variables.R_w_j: response time of the j-th computation segment of tau_3M_plus_2

formal_description.conclusion: Establishes an upper bound on the total response time of tau_3M_plus_2's computation segments when the intermediate-priority interference is not perfectly balanced, but at least one segment receives exactly 'V' units of interference.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma explores what happens to the total response time if the intermediate-priority interference (w_j values) is *not* perfectly balanced (i.e., not all w_j = V), but still sums to M*V, and at least one w_j is exactly V. It shows that any deviation from the perfect balance (w_j = V for all j) will either keep the total response time the same or *decrease* it, relative to the perfectly balanced case (M * (4V + 1)). The proof involves a 'balancing' procedure that moves execution time between segments to reduce the total response time.
steps: Start with an arbitrary distribution of w_j that sums to M*V and has at least one w_j = V.
If any w_j > 2V, redistribute some of its excess to a w_i < V, showing this doesn't increase total R_w_j.
If any w_j > V and some w_i < V, redistribute some of its excess to w_i, showing this doesn't increase total R_w_j.

The process aims to move towards the `w_j = V` for all `j` distribution, or a distribution where `w_j` are either `V` or `V-1` or `V+1` etc. The key is that `R_w_j` is convex-like, so extreme values of `w_j` are 'penalized' more than balanced ones.
The final bound `M * (4V + 1) - V` is derived from this adjustment process, implying that the perfectly balanced case (all w_j = V) maximizes the sum of R_w_j.

def check_lemma_7(M, V, w_values):
    # This lemma describes a property of the R_w_j function's sum
    # The proof involves an iterative adjustment of w_j values.
    # The core idea is that the sum of R_w_j is maximized when w_j are balanced.
    # If sum(w_j) = M*V and at least one w_j = V, then the sum is bounded.
    # The proof is complex and involves showing that moving 'work' from a high R_w_j to a low R_w_j
    # (while maintaining sum(w_j) = M*V) does not increase the total sum.
    pass
key_insights: This lemma demonstrates a crucial property of the R_w_j function: its sum is maximized when the interference is evenly distributed (all w_j = V).
This property is essential for linking the schedulability of tau_3M_plus_2 to the 3-PARTITION problem.

The `M * (4V + 1) - V` bound is slightly less than the perfectly balanced case, indicating that any deviation from perfect balance (while still having one `w_j = V`) leads to a smaller or equal total response time.

results.identifier: Lemma 5 (Condition for tau_3M_plus_2 to miss deadline)

formal_description.statement:
Suppose that T_j is a subset of {tau_2, ..., tau_3M_plus_1} and w_j = sum_{tau_i in T_j} C_i. Task tau_3M_plus_2 misses its deadline in the worst case if and only if there exists a task partition T_1, T_2, ..., T_M such that sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j + sum_{j=1}^{M-1} S_j_3M_plus_2 > D_3M_plus_2.

This is equivalent to: sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j > M * (4V + 1) - V.

variables.tau_3M_plus_2: lowest priority segmented self-suspending task in T_red
variables.T_j: set of intermediate priority tasks interfering with C_j_3M_plus_2
variables.w_j: sum of execution times of tasks in T_j
variables.R_w_j: response time of the j-th computation segment of tau_3M_plus_2

assumptions: Worst-case release pattern as described in Lemma 4.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides the exact condition under which the lowest-priority task tau_3M_plus_2 will miss its deadline, linking it to the sum of response times of its segments and the total suspension time.

informal_sketch.intuition: The lowest-priority task tau_3M_plus_2 will miss its deadline if the total time it takes to complete all its computation segments (sum of R_w_j) plus all its suspension intervals (sum of S_j_3M_plus_2) exceeds its overall deadline (D_3M_plus_2). The lemma simplifies this by showing that this happens if and only if the sum of R_w_j exceeds a specific threshold related to V and M.
steps: Calculate the total time required for tau_3M_plus_2: `Total_Time = sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j + sum_{j=1}^{M-1} S_j_3M_plus_2`.
Compare `Total_Time` with `D_3M_plus_2`.
If `Total_Time > D_3M_plus_2`, the deadline is missed.
Substitute the known values for `D_3M_plus_2` and `S_j_3M_plus_2` from Definition 2 into the inequality.
This substitution leads to the simplified condition: `sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j > M * (4V + 1) - V`.
key_insights: This lemma provides the direct link between the response times of individual segments and the overall schedulability of the segmented self-suspending task.
The simplified condition `sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j > M * (4V + 1) - V` is the key to connecting to the 3-PARTITION problem.

results.identifier: Theorem 1 (coN P-hardness of schedulability analysis for FP)

formal_description.statement: The schedulability analysis for FP scheduling even with only one segmented self-suspending task as the lowest-priority task in the sporadic task system is coN P-hard in the strong sense, when the number of self-suspending intervals in the self-suspending task is more than or equal to 2 and D_i <= T_i for every task tau_i.
assumptions: Task system contains at least one segmented self-suspending task as the lowest priority.
The lowest-priority task has at least 2 self-suspension intervals (or 3 computation segments).
formal_description.conclusion: Proves that determining schedulability for this specific class of self-suspending task systems is computationally intractable (coN P-hard in the strong sense).

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem states that even in a simplified scenario (only one self-suspending task, and it's the lowest priority), figuring out if a task set is schedulable under fixed-priority scheduling is extremely difficult. It's as hard as solving the 3-PARTITION problem, which is known to be intractable.
steps: The proof uses a reduction from the 3-PARTITION problem (Definition 1).
An instance of 3-PARTITION is transformed into a task set T_red (Definition 2) in polynomial time.
Lemma 3 ensures that all higher-priority tasks in T_red are schedulable.
Lemma 4 defines the worst-case scenario for the lowest-priority task tau_3M_plus_2.
Lemma 5 states that tau_3M_plus_2 misses its deadline if and only if `sum_{j=1}^{M} R_w_j > M * (4V + 1) - V`.
The core of the proof is showing that a feasible solution to the 3-PARTITION problem exists if and only if tau_3M_plus_2 is *not* schedulable (i.e., it misses its deadline).

If a 3-PARTITION solution exists, then we can assign `w_j = V` for all `j`. By Lemma 6, `sum R_w_j = M * (4V + 1)`. This value is greater than `M * (4V + 1) - V` (since V > 0), so tau_3M_plus_2 misses its deadline.
If no 3-PARTITION solution exists, then no assignment of `w_j` will result in all `w_j = V`. By Lemma 7, `sum R_w_j <= M * (4V + 1) - V`. This means tau_3M_plus_2 meets its deadline.
Since solving 3-PARTITION is NP-hard, and this reduction shows an equivalence to the *complement* of schedulability (i.e., non-schedulability), the schedulability problem is coN P-hard.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def schedulability_analysis_is_coNP_hard():
    # This is a theoretical proof, not an algorithm.
    # It demonstrates that a function like:
    # def is_schedulable_FP_segmented_lowest_priority(task_set):
    #    # ... (complex analysis) ...
    #    return True/False
    # would be coNP-hard in the strong sense.
    pass
key_insights: This is a strong negative result, indicating that finding an exact (or even pseudo-polynomial time) schedulability test for this class of tasks is highly unlikely.
The complexity arises from the interaction between the partitioning of intermediate-priority tasks and the non-linear response time function of the self-suspending task.
The reduction relies on the specific properties of the R_w_j function and its sum.

results.identifier: Corollary 1 (coN P-hardness of feasible priority assignment)

formal_description.statement: Validating whether there exists a feasible priority assignment is coN P-hard in the strong sense for constrained-deadline segmented self-suspending task systems.
formal_description.conclusion: Proves that finding an optimal priority assignment for this class of tasks is computationally intractable.

informal_sketch.intuition: Not only is it hard to check if a system is schedulable with a *given* priority assignment (Theorem 1), it's also hard to figure out if *any* priority assignment exists that would make the system schedulable. This means the 'scheduler design problem' (finding a good priority assignment) is also intractable.
steps: Theorem 1 proves that checking schedulability for a *fixed* priority assignment (where tau_3M_plus_2 is lowest) is coN P-hard.
In the constructed task set T_red (Definition 2), tau_1 must be the highest priority due to its tight deadline (D_1 = V, C_1 = V).
tau_3M_plus_2 must be the lowest priority because its period T_3M_plus_2 = 21MV is much larger than other tasks, and its deadline D_3M_plus_2 is also large, making it suitable for low priority.
If tau_3M_plus_2 were assigned a higher priority, it would likely cause higher-priority tasks to miss their deadlines due to its long suspension times or large execution demands.
Therefore, the only 'feasible' priority assignment for T_red (if one exists) would be the one used in Theorem 1's proof.
Since checking schedulability for *that specific* assignment is coN P-hard, checking if *any* such assignment exists is also coN P-hard.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_feasible_priority_assignment_is_coNP_hard():
    # This is a theoretical proof, not an algorithm.
    # It implies that a function like:
    # def find_feasible_priority_assignment(task_set):
    #    # ... (search for priority assignment) ...
    #    return priority_assignment_or_None
    # would be coNP-hard in the strong sense.
    pass
key_insights: This extends the negative complexity result from schedulability testing to the problem of designing the scheduler itself (i.e., finding a priority order).
It highlights the fundamental difficulty of managing self-suspending tasks in fixed-priority systems.

formal_description.statement:
A specific task set T_negative with two implicit-deadline tasks:
- Task tau_1: T_1 = D_1 = 1, S_1 = 0, C_1 = B.
- Task tau_2: T_2 = D_2 = 1 / B_power_2, S_2 = (1 / B_power_2) * (1 - B), C_2 = 1.

variables.B: a parameter (0 < B <= 0.25, 1/B is a positive integer)

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific two-task system used to demonstrate unbounded speedup factors.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a specially crafted two-task system. Task tau_1 is a small, frequent, non-suspending task. Task tau_2 is a large, infrequent, self-suspending task. The parameter 'B' allows us to make tau_1 arbitrarily small and frequent, which will be key to showing unbounded speedup factors.
steps: Define tau_1 with period/deadline 1, no suspension, and execution time B.
Define tau_2 with a much larger period/deadline (1/B^2), significant suspension time, and execution time 1.
Note the constraint on B, especially that 1/B is an integer, which simplifies some calculations.
key_insights: The relative scales of C, S, D, T for tau_1 and tau_2 are crucial.
As B approaches 0, tau_1 becomes very light but very frequent, while tau_2's period and suspension time become extremely large.
This task set will be used to show that common scheduling algorithms fail, while a custom algorithm can succeed with a certain speedup.

formal_description.statement:
Algorithm R is a scheduling algorithm specifically designed for task set T_negative:
- An unfinished job of task tau_1 is executed at time t if:
  1) task tau_2 suspends at time t, OR
  2) the laxity of the job of task tau_1 at time t equals 0.
- Otherwise, an unfinished job of task tau_2 is executed at time t.

Laxity of a job of task tau_1 at time t is defined as d_j - t - c_star, where d_j is the absolute deadline of the job and c_star is the remaining execution time of the job.

variables.c_star: remaining execution time of a job

assumptions: Applies only to Task Set T_negative.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines a custom scheduling policy for T_negative that prioritizes tau_1 only under specific conditions, otherwise prioritizing tau_2.

informal_sketch.intuition: Algorithm R tries to prioritize the long-running task tau_2, but it will preempt tau_2 to run tau_1 if tau_2 is suspending anyway, or if tau_1 is about to miss its deadline (laxity is zero). This strategy aims to keep tau_2 running as much as possible while still ensuring tau_1 meets its critical deadlines.
steps: At any time 't', check if tau_1 has an unfinished job.
If tau_1's job is active, check two conditions:
1. Is tau_2 currently in a suspension phase? If yes, run tau_1.
2. Is tau_1's laxity (time remaining until deadline minus remaining execution) zero? If yes, run tau_1.
If neither of these conditions is met (meaning tau_2 is active and tau_1 is not critically urgent), then run tau_2.
Laxity calculation: `deadline - current_time - remaining_execution_time`.
key_insights: This algorithm is designed to be 'smart' about when to prioritize tau_1, specifically to avoid unnecessary preemption of tau_2.
The laxity-based preemption ensures tau_1's deadline is met.
The suspension-based preemption allows tau_1 to utilize processor time that tau_2 would otherwise waste.

formal_description.statement:
Suppose that a job of task tau_1 arrives at time a_j on a processor with speed 1/s and the unfinished job of task tau_2 (arrived before a_j) has not yet finished at time a_j + 1 in the schedule by using Algorithm R. Then, in the schedule by using Algorithm R:
- Case 1: either task tau_2 is executed for exactly 1 - B*s amount of execution time in the time interval [a_j, a_j + 1) and task tau_2 is executed again right at time a_j + 1, OR
- Case 2: or task tau_2 is executed for y amount execution time in the time interval [a_j, a_j + 1) and suspends itself for 1 - y amount of time for some y with 0 <= y <= 1 - B*s.

variables.a_j: arrival time of a job of tau_1
variables.y: amount of execution time for tau_2

assumptions: Task Set T_negative is being scheduled by Algorithm R.
Processor speed is 1/s (meaning C_1 becomes B*s, C_2 becomes 1*s).
A job of tau_1 arrives at a_j.
An unfinished job of tau_2 is active and not finished by a_j + 1.
formal_description.conclusion: Describes the two possible execution patterns for tau_2 within a 1-unit time interval starting at a tau_1 job arrival, given that tau_2 is not yet finished.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma analyzes how Algorithm R behaves within a 1-unit time window (which is tau_1's period) when a tau_1 job arrives and tau_2 is still running. It says that either tau_1 runs for its full (scaled) execution time (B*s) and tau_2 fills the rest, or tau_2 suspends for some part of the interval, allowing tau_1 to run for less than its full time.
steps: Consider the interval [a_j, a_j + 1).
tau_1's execution time at speed 1/s is B*s.
If tau_1's laxity becomes 0, it preempts tau_2. This means tau_1 runs for B*s, and tau_2 runs for `1 - B*s`. This is Case 1.

If tau_1's laxity does not become 0, then tau_2 runs unless it suspends. If tau_2 suspends, tau_1 can run. This is Case 2, where tau_2 runs for `y` and suspends for `1 - y`. The maximum `y` is `1 - B*s` because tau_1 would run for `B*s` if tau_2 didn't suspend and tau_1's laxity became 0.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def analyze_algorithm_R_interval(job_tau_1, job_tau_2, a_j, s, B):
    tau_1_exec_time_scaled = B * s
    # Case 1: tau_1 runs for its full scaled time
    # This happens if tau_1's laxity hits 0, or tau_2 suspends and tau_1 uses the time.
    # If tau_1 runs for tau_1_exec_time_scaled, then tau_2 runs for 1 - tau_1_exec_time_scaled.
    # Case 2: tau_2 suspends for some time.
    # If tau_2 suspends for 'susp_dur', then tau_1 runs for 'tau_1_exec_time_scaled' or less.
    # tau_2 runs for 'y' and suspends for '1-y'.
    # The key is that tau_2's execution + suspension in [a_j, a_j+1) is at most 1, and tau_1 takes B*s if needed.
key_insights: This lemma formalizes the interaction between tau_1 and tau_2 under Algorithm R.
It shows that tau_1 effectively 'claims' B*s of processor time in each of its periods, either by executing or by forcing tau_2 to suspend.
This is crucial for calculating the total available time for tau_2.

formal_description.statement:
Suppose that a job of task tau_1 arrives at time a_j on a processor with speed 1/s and the unfinished job of task tau_2 (arrived before a_j) finishes at time f in time interval [a_j, a_j + 1) in the schedule by using Algorithm R. Then, in the schedule by using Algorithm R:
- Case 3: task tau_2 is executed for y amount execution time in the time interval [a_j, a_j + 1) and suspends itself for f - a_j - y amount of time for some y with 0 <= y < 1 - B*s.

variables.a_j: arrival time of a job of tau_1
variables.y: amount of execution time for tau_2

assumptions: Task Set T_negative is being scheduled by Algorithm R.
A job of tau_1 arrives at a_j.
An unfinished job of tau_2 finishes within [a_j, a_j + 1).
formal_description.conclusion: Describes the execution pattern for tau_2 within a 1-unit time interval when tau_2's job completes within that interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is similar to Lemma 8, but specifically for the case where tau_2 finishes its job within the 1-unit interval starting at a tau_1 job arrival. It implies that tau_2 might not use up all the time available to it (1 - B*s) before finishing.
steps: Consider the interval [a_j, a_j + 1).
tau_2 finishes at time 'f' within this interval.
tau_2 executes for 'y' time and suspends for `f - a_j - y` time.
Since tau_2 finishes, it doesn't necessarily use up all the `1 - B*s` time that would be available if tau_1 ran for its minimum. So `y` can be less than `1 - B*s`.

def analyze_algorithm_R_finish_interval(job_tau_1, job_tau_2, a_j, f, s, B):
    tau_1_exec_time_scaled = B * s
    # If tau_2 finishes at 'f' within [a_j, a_j+1):
    # tau_2's execution 'y' + suspension 'f - a_j - y' = f - a_j.
    # Since tau_2 finishes, it might not have used all the time it could have.
    # So 'y' is less than the maximum available (1 - tau_1_exec_time_scaled).
key_insights: This lemma covers the termination condition for tau_2's job within a tau_1 period.
It ensures that the analysis of available time for tau_2 is consistent even when it completes its work.

results.identifier: Lemma 10 (Deadline miss for T_negative under specific conditions)

formal_description.statement: For task set T_negative, from time 0 to time (1 / B_power_2) * (1 - B), if the jobs of task tau_1 are always with higher priority than the job of task tau_2, then either task tau_1 or task tau_2 misses its deadline.
assumptions: Fixed-priority scheduling where tau_1 has higher priority than tau_2.
Specific job release pattern for tau_2 (defined in the 'Unbounded Scheduling Algorithms' section, not formally extracted here but implicitly assumed for the proof).
0 < epsilon < B_power_3 (epsilon is a small execution time for tau_2's segments).
formal_description.conclusion: Demonstrates that if tau_1 is always higher priority, a deadline miss will occur for T_negative within a specific time interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma shows that if we simply give tau_1 (the small, frequent task) higher priority over tau_2 (the large, self-suspending task), it leads to a deadline miss. The frequent preemption by tau_1 prevents tau_2 from making enough progress, or tau_1 itself might miss its deadline if tau_2's suspension pattern is 'unlucky'.
steps: Assume tau_1 has higher priority than tau_2.
Consider a specific, 'adversarial' job release pattern for tau_2, where it has many small computation segments followed by suspensions.
When tau_1 runs, it preempts tau_2. Since tau_1 is very frequent (period 1), it will frequently preempt tau_2.
The proof analyzes the cumulative blocking of tau_2 by tau_1 over a long interval `(1 / B_power_2) * (1 - B)`.

It shows that either tau_1 cannot complete its execution within its deadline due to tau_2's suspension pattern, or tau_2 is blocked so much by tau_1 that it cannot complete its required execution and suspension within its deadline.
The specific values of C_1, S_2, T_1, T_2 are chosen such that this conflict is unavoidable.

def check_lemma_10(task_set_negative, epsilon):
    tau_1 = task_set_negative.tau_1
    tau_2 = task_set_negative.tau_2
    B = task_set_negative.B

    # Simulate fixed-priority with tau_1 > tau_2
    # Use the specific adversarial job pattern for tau_2
    # Check if tau_1 misses deadline or tau_2 misses deadline
    # The proof involves calculating accumulated execution/blocking over time.
    # It shows that the total demand for processor time by tau_1 and tau_2's active segments
    # exceeds the available time, leading to a miss.
    return True # A deadline miss will occur
key_insights: This lemma demonstrates the inadequacy of simple fixed-priority assignment for T_negative.
It highlights the challenge of scheduling self-suspending tasks, where the 'optimal' priority might not be obvious.
The specific interval `(1 / B_power_2) * (1 - B)` is chosen to expose the worst-case interaction.

results.identifier: Theorem 2 (Algorithm R can feasibly schedule T_negative at reduced speed)

formal_description.statement: Algorithm R can feasibly schedule task tau_1 and task tau_2 on a processor with speed s = 2B * ((1/B) - 0.5) / ((1/B) - 1).
assumptions: Processor speed is 1/s (meaning C_i becomes C_i * s, S_i remains S_i).
0 < B <= 0.25 and 1/B is a positive integer.
formal_description.conclusion: Proves that the specific task set T_negative can be scheduled by Algorithm R if the processor runs at a certain speed 's'.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem shows that even though T_negative is hard to schedule with standard algorithms, a specially designed algorithm (Algorithm R) can schedule it if the processor is sped up by a factor 's'. This 's' value will be used to establish a lower bound on the speedup factor for other algorithms.
steps: First, show tau_1 is schedulable: Algorithm R ensures tau_1 always meets its deadline by prioritizing it when its laxity is zero. This requires `B*s <= 1` (scaled execution time of tau_1 must be <= its deadline).

No matter how fast you make the processor, there will always be a task set (like T_negative with a very small B) that an optimal scheduler could handle on a unit-speed processor, but fixed-priority scheduling cannot, unless the processor is sped up by an enormous (unbounded) factor.
